\chapter{Five Ways to Be}
\label{ch:nervioso-y-listo}
\hlchaptermodality{326}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I am nervous, brave, alone, free or ready in Spanish, and say why ser listo and estar listo mean two different things.}

Complete ES-C326-listo: answer with nervioso or valiente, say estoy solo and estoy libre, and split ser listo from estar listo.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nervioso]{nervioso — an ending you already own, on a fibre you already have}

\label{lesson:ES-C326-nervioso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the square}, then \emph{another place}. (\emph{La plaza}; \emph{otro lugar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item -oso — the ending that answers to English \emph{-ous}.
  \item estar — the verb this word takes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ner-BYO-so}, the weight on the third-from-last beat. The \emph{v} is soft, made without the lips quite meeting, and \emph{io} glides through as one. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{nervioso} — \textquotedblleft{}nervous.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{nervus} was not a nerve. It was a \emph{sinew} — a tendon, a bowstring, the tough cord that makes a thing pull. Its Greek twin is \textbf{neûron}, the same word on the other side of the sea, which is why English ended up with \textbf{nerve} from the Latin and \textbf{neuron}, \textbf{neurology} and \textbf{neurotic} from the Greek.

\emph{Nervōsus} therefore meant \emph{full of sinew} — strong, tough, wiry. English kept that older sense a long while: \emph{nervous} prose is still prose with muscle in it. Only when doctors began calling the body's signalling cords \emph{nerves} did the adjective turn inward and start meaning \emph{anxious} in both languages at once.

The build is one you can already take apart. \emph{Nervus} plus the Latin \textbf{-ōsus} gives Spanish \textbf{-oso}, which is the English \textbf{-ous} — the ending behind \emph{famoso} and \emph{famous}, \emph{curioso} and \emph{curious}. And the \emph{-o} switches for a woman: \textbf{nerviosa}.

One thing to fix now. Being nervous is a state you are in, not a thing you are, so it takes \emph{estar}: \textbf{estoy nervioso}, not \emph{soy nervioso}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five ways to answer \emph{¿cómo estás?} with something other than \emph{bien}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nervioso}
  \item \emph{estoy nervioso}
  \item \emph{nervioso — nerviosa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{nervus} before it was a nerve? (A sinew — a bowstring.) And which Spanish verb does \emph{nervioso} take? (\emph{Estar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[valiente]{valiente — the opposite of nervioso, and a verb you already say}

\label{lesson:ES-C326-valiente}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{another place}, then \emph{I am nervous}. (\emph{Otro lugar}; \emph{estoy nervioso}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item más vale pájaro en mano — the \emph{vale} in it is this verb.
  \item triste — the word that showed why an \emph{-e} ending never switches.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ba-LYEN-te}, the weight on the middle beat. The \emph{v} is soft again, and \emph{ie} rides through as one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{valiente} — \textquotedblleft{}brave.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{valēre} meant \emph{to be strong}, and from there \emph{to be worth} — because what is strong is what holds up, and what holds up is what is worth having. Both meanings survived. Spanish \textbf{valer} is \emph{to be worth}, and its old present participle, \emph{the one being strong}, hardened into the adjective \textbf{valiente}.

You have been saying the verb already. In the proverb about the bird in the hand, \emph{más vale} is \emph{is worth more}. And the everyday Spanish \textbf{vale} — \emph{okay}, \emph{fine}, \emph{agreed} — is the same form: \emph{it holds}, \emph{it stands}.

English took the whole family. \textbf{Valiant} is \emph{valiente} through French. \textbf{Valour} is the strength. \textbf{Value} is the worth. Something \textbf{valid} stands up; something \textbf{invalid} does not, and an \emph{invalid} person was once somebody whose strength had gone. To \textbf{prevail} is to be stronger in front. To \textbf{convalesce} is to grow strong together with your body again. Even the Latin farewell \textbf{valē} — \emph{be strong} — is the same word, and it is what the Spanish \emph{vale} is descended from.

It ends in \emph{-e}, so there is nothing to switch: \emph{un chico valiente}, \emph{una chica valiente}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two states that face each other, and a root you can hear in \emph{vale} all day.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{valiente}
  \item \emph{nervioso — valiente}
  \item \emph{una chica valiente}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What were the two meanings of \emph{valēre}? (To be strong, and to be worth.) And why does \emph{valiente} stay the same for a woman? (It ends in \emph{-e}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[solo]{solo — one word, two meanings, and an accent that no longer exists}

\label{lesson:ES-C326-solo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I am nervous}, then \emph{brave}. (\emph{Estoy nervioso}; \emph{valiente}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SO-lo}, two even beats, the weight on the first. Both \emph{o} sounds stay short and pure — Spanish never lets an \emph{o} slide off into a second vowel the way English \emph{go} does. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{solo} — \textquotedblleft{}alone.\textquotedblright{} And also \textquotedblleft{}only.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{sōlus} meant \emph{alone}, and English is full of it. Your \textbf{sole} purpose is your only one. A musician plays a \textbf{solo}, alone. A \textbf{solitary} person keeps to \textbf{solitude}. \textbf{Desolate} ground has been left all alone. A \textbf{soliloquy} is speaking alone on a stage.

Spanish put the one word to two jobs. \emph{Estoy solo} is \emph{I am alone}. \emph{Solo quiero agua} is \emph{I only want water}. Same five letters, two meanings, and for most of the twentieth century Spanish separated them in writing: the \emph{only} one was spelled \textbf{sólo}, with an accent, and the \emph{alone} one was not.

That accent is gone. In 2010 the Royal Spanish Academy ruled it unnecessary, because the sentence around the word already tells you which meaning is running. You will still see \emph{sólo} in older books and from writers who kept the habit, and neither spelling is a mistake to read — but the rule now is that both are written \textbf{solo}.

There is one difference the spelling never showed anyway. \emph{Alone} describes a person, so it switches: a woman says \textbf{estoy sola}. \emph{Only} describes the sentence, not a person, so it never moves: \emph{solo} stays \emph{solo} for everybody.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that does two jobs, and the reason the accent it used to carry was dropped.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{estoy solo}
  \item \emph{estoy sola}
  \item \emph{solo quiero agua}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things can \emph{solo} mean? (Alone, and only.) And which of the two changes to \emph{sola} for a woman? (\emph{Alone} — the \emph{only} one never moves.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[libre]{libre — not the same word as libro, and Spanish keeps them apart}

\label{lesson:ES-C326-libre}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{brave}, then \emph{I only want water}. (\emph{Valiente}; \emph{solo quiero agua}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el libro — close enough to trip you, and a different word underneath.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{LEE-bre}, the weight on the first beat. The \emph{b} is soft between vowels, and the \emph{r} is one flick — hold it any longer and you have said \emph{libre} with a roll it does not want. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{libre} — \textquotedblleft{}free.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had two words spelled \textbf{liber} and they had nothing to do with each other. One was the inner bark of a tree, the surface people wrote on before paper, and it became the word for a book — Spanish \textbf{libro}, English \emph{library}. The other meant \emph{not owned by anybody}: a free person rather than a slave.

Spanish inherited both and kept them clearly apart: \textbf{libro} for the object, \textbf{libre} for the condition. English inherited both too, but sent them to different shelves — \emph{library} from the bark, \textbf{liberty} from the free person — so the collision is invisible until somebody points at it.

The free \emph{liber} is a large family in English. \textbf{Liberty} and \textbf{liberate} are plain. A \textbf{liberal} was originally a free person's education, the kind a citizen rather than a labourer received. And to \textbf{deliver} is \emph{dē-līberāre}, to set free \emph{from} something — which is why a delivery is a parcel released to you.

\emph{Libre} ends in \emph{-e}, so it never switches. And it does one thing English cannot: English \emph{free} covers both \emph{unowned} and \emph{costing nothing}, while Spanish splits them — \textbf{libre} is the first, \textbf{gratis} is the second.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four states, and a pair of look-alikes you will never confuse again.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{libre}
  \item \emph{el libro — libre}
  \item \emph{estoy libre}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Are \emph{libro} and \emph{libre} the same Latin word? (No — one was tree bark, the other meant unowned.) And which Spanish word means \emph{free of charge}? (\emph{Gratis}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[listo]{listo — the word where ser and estar change the meaning outright}

\label{lesson:ES-C326-listo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I am alone}, then \emph{free}. (\emph{Estoy solo}; \emph{libre}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ser vs estar — the split this word finally pays off.
  \item blanco $\leftarrow$ *blank — the Germanic layer of Spanish, already met.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{LEES-to}, the weight on the first beat. No vowel goes in front of the \emph{st} — Spanish usually refuses that cluster at the start of a word, but in the middle it runs clean. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{listo} — \textquotedblleft{}clever,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}ready,\textquotedblright{} and which one depends entirely on the verb.

\textbf{Ser listo} is \emph{to be clever}. That is what somebody is: a standing fact about them. \textbf{Estar listo} is \emph{to be ready}. That is what somebody is right now, and in ten minutes it may have changed.

You were taught the \emph{ser}/\emph{estar} split a long way back as a rule about permanent and temporary. Here is where the rule stops being an abstraction and starts paying rent. With most adjectives, choosing the wrong verb sounds odd. With \emph{listo}, it says something else entirely. \emph{Es lista} praises her mind. \emph{Está lista} means she has her coat on.

The word's own history is a smaller surprise. The Royal Spanish Academy traces \emph{listo} to Gothic \textbf{lists}, \emph{cunning} — Spanish has a Germanic layer left by the Visigoths, and you have met it already in \emph{blanco}, which came from a Germanic \emph{blank} rather than from Latin. German still uses the word: \textbf{List} is a clever trick, and \emph{listig} means crafty. English once had it too, as Old English \emph{list}, \emph{skill} or \emph{craft}, and then let it go — one of the places where Spanish kept a Germanic word that English dropped.

The \emph{-o} switches: \textbf{listo}, \textbf{lista}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five states of mind — and proof that \emph{ser} and \emph{estar} are not decoration.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{estoy listo}
  \item \emph{es listo}
  \item \emph{soy lista, pero no estoy lista}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb makes \emph{listo} mean \emph{clever}? (\emph{Ser}.) And which makes it mean \emph{ready}? (\emph{Estar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
